title: Toronto officers won't be charged in 2016 shooting death of mentally ill Ottawa man
article: The province's Special Investigations Unit has concluded that no charges are warranted in the death of an Ottawa man shot eight times by police in Toronto on March 4, 2016.

Devon LaFleur, 30, was wanted by police in Ottawa for an armed robbery earlier that day and had left the city to head to Toronto in an SUV stolen from his sister to meet a friend. Toronto police, who had been warned that LeFleur was headed to Toronto and were waiting for him, shot LaFleur eight times on Bayview Avenue in North York late that night. He died soon after.

Friends and family have described LaFleur as a gentle man who had struggled with mental illness since early adolescence. His mother, Rena LaFleur, said Monday that her son's schizophrenia was usually under control but that he had not taken his medication.

She added that the family had warned police that LaFleur was carrying a inoperable BB gun and not a real firearm.

Rena LaFleur said her son had previous interactions with Ottawa police - he had been arrested for robberies in 2007 and 2009 - but Ottawa officers knew how to manage him without harm. When Devon headed to Toronto, his family notified police with the understanding was that plainclothes police officers would approach him and take him into custody to be brought to hospital, she said.

"We thought we could trust them to protect him," she said. "Police knew it was highly likely he would be psychotic. They knew it was a mentally ill person headed their way. What happened was uniformed officers and yelling and confrontation. Devon didn't want to die. He may have thought that the bullets couldn't hurt him."

The SIU is an agency that investigates deaths, serious injury or allegations of sexual assault involving police. In a statement released Monday, SIU director Tony Loparco said there was no question that the three officers who shot LaFleur, called "the man" in the report, were acting in the course of their duty.

It took 15 months for the SIU's conclusion to be released. Eight investigators and three forensic investigators were assigned to this case. The SIU interviewed 10 civilian witnesses and nine police officers on the scene, as well as the duty notes of an additional 11 officers, as well as a review of communications between police in Ottawa and Toronto. The report makes no mention of the family's involvement, or their request to send plainclothes officers to intercept LaFleur.

The shooting was the culmination of a chain of events that began after LaFleur stole the SUV and robbed a bank in Kanata on March 4, 2016. Ottawa Police also had relayed information to Toronto that LeFleur had also stolen a pellet gun that closely resembled a real firearm, according to the report.

Ottawa police believed LaFleur was on his way to Toronto to visit a friend and an Ottawa police detective attempted to contact the friend. Ottawa police also gave their colleagues in Toronto a description of LaFleur and said he was armed with a handgun, but added the caveat that his family reported that a pellet gun was missing and it was unclear if the same weapon was used in the robbery.

A Toronto police sergeant contacted LaFleur's friend at about 9:30 p.m., and she reported that she was to meet LaFleur at a shopping mall. Police were dispatched to the mall to look for LaFleur and the stolen vehicle. At about 10 p.m, the friend told police she was in a cab on her way to the address on Bayview Avenue. Officers in three police vehicles were dispatched to Bayview Avenue. Witnesses said the area was well-lit with street lamps.

The police arrived ahead of the cab, which arrived at 10:08 p.m. The friend left the cab and walked to the door of the residence. One officer moved his cruiser behind the cab, a second cruiser moved behind the first and the third cruiser travelled farther south along Bayview Avenue, where the emergency roof lights and in-car camera system were activated.

LaFleur left the cab and stood just outside the door facing the police. Two of the officers in the cruiser closest to the cab stood behind their door. LaFleur began shouting at the police: "What are you going to do?" and held what appeared to be a black handgun at his right side. The first officer drew his firearm and yelled "gun" to the other officers to alert them. The second officer also drew his gun and began yelling police challenges.

The third and fourth officers left their cruiser and also stood behind their doors for cover and drew their firearms, then ran up the driveway to the first cruiser. LaFleur was illuminated by headlights from one of the police vehicles, and the third officer confirmed that he was holding what appeared to be a black handgun. LaFleur continued to shout, "What are you going to do?" and held the gun at his side, according to the report.

LaFleur's friend ran up to him and tried to wrestle the weapon out of his hand. He pushed the woman away, and the officers yelled at her to get away. LaFleur then extended his right arm straight into the air and pointed the gun at the first officer. The first, second and third officers discharged their firearms. The first officer fired 12 or 13 rounds, according to the SIU investigation; the second officer fired eight or nine rounds, and the third officer fired a single shot.
